```{r load packages, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(moderndive)
library(ggplot2)
library(tibble)
```

```{r Problem 1}
#import and quickly view the data
data("early_january_weather")  
skimr::skim(early_january_weather)
#There are 15 variables in this data set

#find the variable names 
names(early_january_weather)
#The names of the variables are  "origin"     "year"       "month"      "day"        "hour"       "temp"       "dewp"       "humid" "wind_dir"   "wind_speed"    "wind_gust"  "precip"     "pressure"   "visib"      "time_hour". For year we can see that it is 2013 for every entry and that temp is in Fahrenheit.

#find number of rows and columns
nrow(early_january_weather) #358 rows
ncol(early_january_weather) #15 columns

#mean temperature
mean(early_january_weather$temp, na.rm = TRUE) #mean temp is 39.58 Fahrenheit.

#Create scatterplot
library(ggplot2)

p <- ggplot(early_january_weather,
            aes(x = hour, y = temp, color = humid)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(title = "Temperature over Time (colored by Humidity)",
       x = "Time (hourly)", 
       y = "Temperature (°F)",
       color = "Humidity")

p

#The scatter plot of temperature (temp) versus hour of day (time_hour), shows a daily cycle. Temps are lowest in the early morning hours and rise through the day, peaking in the afternoon before cooling again at night. Humidity values (shown by color) are higher during cooler nighttime hours (purple/blue points) and lower during warmer daytime hours (yellow/orange points).

#save plot 
ggsave(
  filename = "scatter_temp_time.pdf",  
  plot = p,                            
  width = 8, height = 4, 
  device = "pdf"                       
)
```

```{r Problem 2}
#set seed so values are the same each time
set.seed(123)

#Create data frame
df <- tibble::tibble(
  num_var  = rnorm(10),
  log_var  = num_var > 0,
  char_var = paste0("element_", 1:10),
  fac_var  = factor(rep(c("low","med","high"), length.out = 10))
)

df

#Check mean for each variable 
#numeric: works
mean(df$num_var)

#logical: works (TRUE = 1, FALSE = 0)
mean(df$log_var)

#character: fails
mean(df$char_var)

#factor: fails
mean(df$fac_var)
```

```{r, results='hide'}
#using as.numeric
as.numeric(df$log_var)   
as.numeric(df$char_var)  
as.numeric(df$fac_var)  
```

#When applying as.numeric() to each variable we see that for the logical variable, TRUE values are converted to 1 and FALSE values to 0. This explains why the mean of a logical vector works b/c it is just the proportion of true/1. For the character variable, all entries are converted to NA because characters have no numeric representation and that is why the mean fails bc there is no value to the variable. For the factor variable, the levels are converted to their underlying codes like 1,2,3. This shows why the mean of a factor fails as the integer codes are arbitrary labels and not meaningful values.
